Common questions about our home care in Maidstone and Kent. Can't find what you need? Get in touch and we'll be happy to help.

What areas do you cover?

We provide home care across Maidstone and Kent, including surrounding towns and villages. If you're unsure whether we cover your area, please contact us and we'll confirm.

How quickly can care start?

We aim to arrange a care consultation within a few days of your enquiry. Care often starts within a month of agreeing your plan, so we have time to find the right carers.

Can I have the same carer each time?

Yes. We prioritise consistency so you see familiar faces. We match you with a small team who get to know you and your routine, so you know who is coming.

What types of care do you offer?

We offer domiciliary care (day-to-day support with personal care, medication and companionship), respite care (short breaks for family carers), and complex care (specialist clinical support at home). You can read more on our Our Services page.

How do I pay for care?

Care can be funded privately, through local authority support, or via health funding depending on your situation. We can discuss options during your consultation and signpost you to advice if needed.

Are you regulated by the CQC?

Yes. We are registered with the Care Quality Commission. You can view our latest CQC rating on our CQC and Our Care page or on the CQC website.

What if I need to change or stop care?

You can change your care plan or hours at any time by talking to us. If you need to stop care, we ask for notice where possible so we can support a smooth handover.
new_content:
Common questions about our home care in Maidstone and Kent. Can't find what you need? Get in touch and we'll be happy to help.

What can a carer help me with at home?

Home care can help with everyday things such as getting washed and dressed, preparing meals, moving around and remembering medicines. You might need a little support each week or more regular visits.

We’ll talk about what you’d like help with and what you want to keep doing for yourself.

Read the NHS guide to home care

How do I know which type of care I need?

You don’t need to know the name of a service before asking for help. Start with what’s becoming difficult, what matters to you and what you’d like to stay the same.

Our free consultation is a chance to talk this through. You can also ask your local council for a care needs assessment, which looks at the support you may need.

Find out about a council needs assessment

Can I arrange care without going through the council?

Yes. You can contact a home-care provider directly and pay for your own support. You don’t need a council referral to start that conversation.

A council needs assessment can still be useful, even if you expect to pay for care yourself.

Read the NHS advice on arranging home care

How much does your home care cost?

Our domiciliary and respite care start from £36.38 an hour. Complex care starts from £40.43 an hour.

The support you need will shape the cost. We’ll talk through your requirements during your free consultation so you can understand your options before deciding.

Will I have the same carers?

We plan your care around a small, regular team, rather than promising one person for every visit. This gives carers time to get to know you, your preferences and your routine.

We also fully fund training to develop their skills as your needs change. If we don’t have the right match, we can recruit someone to suit your needs.

Is a council care needs assessment free?

Yes. A council care needs assessment is free, including if you expect to pay for care yourself.

It looks at what support you need. A separate financial assessment considers whether the council will contribute towards the cost. Having an assessment does not mean you must accept care.

Read the NHS guide to needs assessments

Can I get help paying for care at home?

You may be eligible for help from your local council. It will assess your care needs and, where appropriate, your finances to work out whether it will contribute.

Your income, savings and individual circumstances can affect the outcome. Qualifying for support does not necessarily mean all your care will be free.

Read Kent County Council’s funding guidance

Find your council if you live outside the Kent County Council area

Will I have to sell my home to pay for care at home?

For an adult receiving care in their own home, the value of the home they live in is not included in the council’s financial assessment.

Other property, savings and income may be considered. Different rules apply to a permanent move into a care home, so it’s important to look at guidance for your circumstances.

See Kent County Council’s financial assessment guidance

Can direct payments be used to pay for a care agency?

Yes, where this is agreed as part of your care and support plan. Direct payments let you arrange eligible support yourself rather than having the council arrange it for you.

An assessed personal contribution may still apply. Check that your chosen support and its cost fit the agreed arrangements before committing.

Read about direct payments in Kent

Could the NHS pay for care at home?

Some adults with a “primary health need” qualify for NHS Continuing Healthcare. This can fund an assessed package of care at home and is not means-tested.

Eligibility depends on an assessment of your overall needs, not a diagnosis alone. Ask your GP, nurse or social worker whether an assessment may be appropriate.

Read the NHS guide to Continuing Healthcare

Can I get support so I can take a break from caring?

Yes. Respite care provides support for the person you care for while you take some time away, whether to rest, attend appointments or make plans of your own.

If you’re an adult caring for another adult without pay, you can ask your council for a free carer’s assessment. This looks at your needs too. Any support or funding offered depends on your circumstances.

Read about respite care

Find out about a carer’s assessment

What if my relative doesn’t want care?

It can be difficult when you’re worried about someone and they don’t want support. Start by listening to their concerns and asking what, if anything, they would find helpful.

An adult who has the mental capacity to make a particular care decision can refuse support. A decision others disagree with does not, by itself, mean someone lacks capacity. Being a relative does not automatically give you authority to decide for them.

Read the NHS guidance on mental capacity and decision-making

Where can I ask about support for my disabled child?

Contact your council’s children’s services to ask about an assessment of your child’s support needs. Explain what daily life is like, what your child needs help with and how caring affects your family.

Children’s support follows a different assessment route from adult social care. Medway has its own council services, separate from Kent County Council.

Ask Kent County Council about support for your child

Find children’s social care information in Medway

What should I check when choosing a home-care provider?

Look at the provider’s CQC registration, rating and latest inspection report. Then ask practical questions: who will visit, how carers are matched, what happens if someone is unavailable, what the charges cover and how to raise a concern.

Think about whether the team listens to you and explains things clearly, as well as the services it offers.

Find home-care agencies and inspection reports on the CQC website
